guide.approve.body:
**To decide on a week:**

1. Open **Approvals**. Weeks waiting for you are at the top.
2. Check the hours. A week flagged **now …** has changed since it was submitted; look at it before accepting.
3. Press **Approve**, or write a reason and press **Send back**.

A reason is required to send a week back. "Rejected" on its own leaves the person guessing, and they will simply submit the same hours again.

**You cannot decide on your own week**, whatever your role. An administrator working on a project still cannot sign off their own hours.

**To correct an approved week**, find it under **Approved weeks** and press **Reopen**. It goes back to its owner to fix. Reopening is recorded with who did it and why - it is meant to be possible, and visible.

**To see who has not submitted at all**, open the **Approval status** report from the Approvals screen. It shows every person against every week, and marks the weeks with time recorded but nothing handed in. A submission that was never made has no entry in the queue, so the queue cannot show you this.
guide.approve.summary: Accept, send back, or reopen a colleague's timesheet.
guide.approve.title: Approving somebody's week
guide.backup.body:
On the **Backup** screen:

1. Choose what to include - everything, or narrow it to one customer, one project or a date range.
2. Press **Download backup**. You get a single zip archive holding the data as JSON, a readme, and every attachment in its original form. A backup with a timesheet and no receipts is not a backup: the evidence behind a billed expense has to travel with it.

**To encrypt it**, set a backup password in **Settings**. Every archive is then encrypted with AES-256, and any archiver that handles encrypted zip files will open it - 7-Zip, WinZip, Keka and most desktop archive managers. Do this before putting a backup anywhere you would not put the database itself: it carries every note, rate and receipt in one file. The password does not protect the database, only copies of the archive that have left this machine.

**To restore**, choose the file and upload it. An encrypted archive needs the same password set in Settings on the machine you are restoring to. Restoring **merges**: it adds what is missing and leaves alone what is already there. Restoring the same file twice creates nothing the second time, and restoring an older backup does not remove newer work.

Plain JSON backups from earlier versions still restore.

A backup written by a newer version of the application is refused rather than partly read.

**Automatic backups** can be turned on with an interval and a number to keep. They are written to the data directory; copy them somewhere else, because a backup on the same disk as the original is not a backup.
guide.backup.summary: Take a copy of your data, and put it back.
guide.backup.title: Backing up and restoring
guide.calendar.body:
1. Export your calendar. In Outlook: **File → Save Calendar**. In Google Calendar: **Settings → Import & export → Export**. Both give you an `.ics` file.
2. Go to **Import → Import a calendar**, choose the file, and optionally pick an assignment to use for meetings that match nothing.
3. Review the list. Nothing is recorded yet.
4. Tick what was actually work, set each one's assignment, and import.

**A calendar is not a timesheet**, which is why the review step exists. The list shows every event in the file, including the ones that will not be imported and why: cancelled meetings, meetings you declined, all-day entries like public holidays, and repeating series — only the one occurrence in the file is there, so it is left for you to decide about.

Meetings are matched to assignments by their words. If a meeting names one assignment it is filled in; if it names a project with several assignments it is left for you, because guessing would put the hour on the wrong invoice.

Exporting again next month is safe: anything already imported is marked and not pre-selected.
guide.calendar.summary: Bring meetings in from Outlook or Google.
guide.calendar.title: Importing from a calendar
guide.correct.body:
The commonest mistake is a length in the wrong unit: `8m` typed where `8h` was meant. To fix it:

1. Find the entry on **Today** or **Entries**.
2. Press the pencil at the end of its row.
3. Change what is wrong and press **Save**.

The length is shown in the same notation it accepts - `8m`, `1h 30m`, `8h` - so what is on screen can be typed straight back.

The **end time** is left empty on purpose. If you fill it in, it is used *instead of* the length, so a prefilled one would quietly throw away the length you had just corrected. Leave it empty unless you specifically want to set an end time.

Changing the date moves the entry to that day. If it moves it into a different week, both weeks have to be open.

Every change is recorded, including what the value was before, so a figure that has been corrected can still be explained later.

If the week has been submitted or approved you cannot change anything in it. Withdraw the submission yourself, or ask a manager to reopen an approved week.
guide.correct.summary: Change a length, a day, an assignment or a note after the fact.
guide.correct.title: Fixing an entry
guide.expenses.body:
On the **Expenses** screen:

1. Choose the project the cost belongs to and the date it was spent.
2. Describe it, and either type the amount or choose how it is priced - **Distance (km)** or **Days** - and give the quantity.
3. Tick **Billable** if the customer is invoiced for it, **Reimbursable** if you are paid back. They are independent questions: a cost can be one, both, or neither.
4. Add it, then attach the receipt to the row.

**Mileage and per diem** are priced from the customer's own rate, so give the distance and the amount is worked out. Nobody should be multiplying 42.5 by 2.50 in their head.

**Markup** applies only to the billable side. What you are paid back is always what it cost.

**Receipts.** Photograph the receipt and paste it straight onto the row - the whole row accepts a pasted image - or use the file button. If the customer requires receipts above an amount, a claim without one is marked and your week cannot be submitted until it has one.
guide.expenses.summary: Costs, receipts, mileage and per diem.
guide.expenses.title: Claiming an expense
guide.export.body:
Everything is exported from the **Entries** screen, so what you download is exactly what is on screen - including the search box and every filter, not just the dates.

1. Set the filter: dates, customer, project, assignment, kind, tags, billable, or a search.
2. Choose a format from the export bar.

**PDF** and **Word** for sending to a client: grouped by customer and project, with subtotals, and a note on any line billed at something other than the base rate so a figure can be explained from the document it appears on.

**Markdown** for pasting a week into a ticket, a wiki, a pull request or an email. Its tables are lined up in the source too, so it stays readable in the places that never render it.

**CSV** for a spreadsheet or an invoicing system. It carries a byte order mark, so Excel on Windows reads non-ASCII names correctly.

**JSON** for another system to read. It follows a documented, versioned schema and carries both the recorded and the billable duration along with the rounding rule that produced each figure, so the arithmetic can be checked rather than trusted.

The filter lives in the address bar, so a filtered view can be bookmarked or sent to a colleague.
guide.export.summary: PDF, Word, Markdown, CSV and JSON, for invoicing or for a client.
guide.export.title: Getting the data out
guide.find.body:
**Search** on the **Entries** screen matches anywhere in the note, the assignment, the project, the customer or the tags. Fragments work: `redir` finds "fixed the login redirect". What you type is searched for literally, so `C++` finds C++.

A search of one or two characters cannot use the index and is scanned instead. The screen says which happened, so two similar searches behaving differently is never a mystery.

**Regular expressions**: tick the box beside the search field. Patterns are RE2 syntax and ignore case; use `(?-i)` if you need case to matter.

**Tags** are labels that cut across customers and projects: `#incident`, `#onboarding`, `#billable-review`.

1. Add one by typing `#incident` into quick-add, or into the Tags field when correcting an entry.
2. That creates it — there is no separate step.
3. Click a tag on any row to see everything carrying it, or type it into the Tags filter.

Filtering by two tags finds entries carrying **both**. Rename, recolour or remove tags on the **Tags** screen; the entry count there tells you which are still earning their keep.

**Results are shown fifty at a time**, with the total beside them, and the pager carries whatever you filtered by - so moving to the next page keeps your search rather than dropping it.

**An export always covers the whole filter, not the page on screen.** Filter to what you want to bill, then download; the file contains every matching entry however many pages the screen split them across.
guide.find.title: Finding an entry
guide.intro: How to do the everyday things. The ? button on each screen explains what you are looking at; this explains how to get something done.
guide.move.body:
Editing one entry changes one entry. When a whole afternoon went on the wrong assignment, use **Move** instead:

1. Go to **Entries** and filter down to what you want to move - a date range, a customer, an assignment.
2. Select the entries.
3. Choose the assignment they should have been on, and confirm.

Moving re-prices the time, because the new assignment may belong to a customer with a different rate. The move is recorded, so the old and new placement are both explicable afterwards.

Entries in a submitted or approved week are skipped rather than moved. Nothing in a locked week changes.
guide.move.summary: When hours went on the wrong assignment, project or customer.
guide.move.title: Moving time to the right place
guide.proxy.body:
Sometimes you have to record time in somebody else's name: they are on site, they are ill, the week closes tonight. You can, and what you record is a **proposal** until they accept it.

That is the whole design. Time recorded in your name that you did not enter must never simply appear as though you had entered it - it is your timesheet, it may be approved and invoiced, and you have to have agreed to it.

**To propose time for a colleague:**

1. You must both be members of the same project. If you are not, ask an administrator to add you.
2. On **Today**, use the quick-add box and add `@name`: `3h acme/support @erik incident call`. Or open **Add time manually** and choose the colleague in the **on behalf of** field.
3. Send it. The entry now sits in their **Inbox** marked **pending**.

**What happens then.** Until they decide, the entry:

- counts towards no total, no report and no export;
- appears on their day view marked **pending** and showing that you entered it;
- shows in your own list the same way, so you can see it is still waiting.

**When they look at their Inbox** they can accept it, correct it and accept it, or reject it with a reason. A rejection is kept rather than deleted: the record of what was claimed has to survive the disagreement.

If your proposal overlaps another one for the same person, both are flagged so they can see it before accepting.

**To accept time somebody proposed for you**, open **Inbox** from the navigation - the badge shows how many are waiting - and accept, edit, or reject each one.
guide.proxy.summary: Enter somebody else's hours — and why they have to agree.
guide.proxy.title: Recording time for a colleague
guide.record.body:
**As you work.** On the **Today** screen, press the assignment you are about to work on under **Start**. The timer runs in the header. Press **Stop** when you finish.

Several timers can run at once, and they are allowed to overlap - a build running for one client while a meeting for another is under way is real, and the tool does not pretend otherwise. The **Tracked** total is the sum of your entries and is what gets billed; **Covered** is how much of the day they span. They differ when work overlapped, which is why both are shown.

**Afterwards.** Type it into the quick-add box at the top of the day:

1. Start with the length or a time range: `2h`, `90m`, `1.5`, or `9:00-10:30`.
2. Name the assignment: `acme/migration`. Part of the name is enough; it matches against what you have worked on recently.
3. Everything left over is the note.

So `2h acme/migration fixed the login redirect` records two hours. If anything is ambiguous you get an error rather than a guess - a wrong guess that quietly becomes billable time is worse than typing it again.

**By hand.** Open **Add time manually** at the foot of the day for a form with the date, start time, length, note and kind of time.

**Kind of time.** Work, overtime or travel. Many contracts pay differently for each, and the customer's terms decide what yours is worth. Nothing is reclassified for you: if a customer has agreed a limit, you get a reminder on the week view and you decide.
guide.record.summary: As you work, or afterwards from memory.
guide.record.title: Recording time
guide.repeat.body:
Most time is not novel: the same few assignments, the same stand-up, the same lunch. Retyping it is what makes people give up on recording as they go.

**One-click starts.** The row of buttons under the date is what you work on most — your favourites first, then whatever you have used most in the last six weeks. Press one to start a timer on it.

**Switch to something else.** With a timer running, each button also gets a ⇄ control. That stops everything running and starts the one you pressed, in a single action. Use the plain button instead when you genuinely want two timers at once — that is allowed and often right.

**Copy yesterday.** At the foot of the day, **Copy yesterday** brings across every entry from the previous day with its time, length, note and tags. On the week view, **Copy last week** does the same for a whole week, day for day. Both add to what is already there rather than replacing it.

**Routines** are for what recurs: lunch, the stand-up, Friday admin.

1. Go to **Routines** and add one: a name, an assignment, which weekdays, a length, and optionally a start time and tags.
2. On any day it applies to, it appears under **Due today**. One click records it.
3. **Add all** records everything outstanding for that day.

Nothing is created on its own. A routine is a way of typing, not a schedule — the tool will not record an hour you did not work because the calendar said Tuesday.
guide.repeat.summary: Copy a day, set up a routine, switch timers.
guide.repeat.title: Recording the same thing again
guide.setup.body:
Work is organised in three levels: a **customer** is who is invoiced, a **project** is a body of work for them, and an **assignment** is what a timer actually runs against.

1. On **Admin**, add the customer with its currency and default hourly rate.
2. Add a project under it, and an assignment under the project.
3. Give the assignment a colour and an icon - that is what makes the day view scannable.

**Rates are inherited.** An assignment uses its own rate if it has one, otherwise the person's rate on that project, otherwise the project's, otherwise the customer's. Set the rate at the level it is actually agreed at and leave the rest empty.

**Rounding** is set per project - to the quarter hour, or a minimum of two, four or eight hours per entry - and is applied when the entry is recorded, never when a report is run.

**Contract terms.** Press **Contract** on a customer for the terms beyond the base rate: overtime as a rate or a percentage, travel time at its own rate or not billed at all, expense markup, mileage and per diem, and whether receipts are required above an amount. Everything there is optional.

Nothing is ever deleted, only archived: removing a customer would leave last year's invoices unable to say who was billed.
guide.setup.summary: Customers, projects, assignments, rates and what the contract says.
guide.setup.title: Setting up customers and contract terms
guide.submit.body:
Submitting a week says "these are my hours". To do it:

1. Go to **Week** and check the totals.
2. Deal with anything the screen is telling you: unaccounted gaps, entries needing review, overtime that is not marked, expenses missing a receipt.
3. Press **Submit week**.

**The week is then locked.** Nothing in it can be added, edited, moved or deleted, and no timer can be started inside it. That is the point: hours that keep changing afterwards are not a declaration.

**If you remember something afterwards**, press **Withdraw** on the week view. That is yours to do as long as nobody has decided yet - you do not need a manager for it.

**If it comes back.** A manager can send a week back with a reason. The reason appears on your week view. Fix what it says and submit again.

**Once it is approved** you can no longer withdraw it. Ask a manager to reopen the week; that is a deliberate act and it is recorded.

A week with nothing in it cannot be submitted, and if your customer requires receipts above an amount, a claim without one will stop the submission until you attach it.
guide.submit.summary: Hand your hours in, and what you can still change afterwards.
guide.submit.title: Submitting your week
guide.title: How to
help.admin.body:
Three levels: a **customer** is who gets billed, a **project** is a body of work for them, and an **assignment** is the thing a timer actually runs against — the granularity people describe their day in.

Colours and icons are not decoration. They are what makes the day view scannable at a glance, and the colour is stored as a palette name rather than a fixed value so it stays legible in all seven themes.

Nothing here is ever deleted, only archived. Deleting a customer would leave last year's invoice unable to say who was billed.

Rates resolve from the most specific level outwards: assignment, then the person's rate on the project, then the project, then the customer, then the instance default. The rate and the rounding rule are copied onto each entry when it is billed, so changing a rate tomorrow cannot alter what was invoiced today.
help.admin.title: Customers, projects and assignments
help.approvals.body:
A week is the unit that gets declared finished. Submitting one says "these are my hours" and locks the week to you: time in it cannot be added, edited, moved or deleted while the lock holds.

A submission that has not been decided can be **withdrawn** by the person who made it - people remember something after they submit, and needing a manager to undo that makes them submit late instead.

Only a manager approves, and never their own week, whatever their role. A rejection needs a reason, because "rejected" on its own leaves the owner guessing and they will simply resubmit the same hours.

An approved week can be **reopened**. It is a deliberate act and it is recorded, which is better than the alternative: a system with no way back forces people to correct a mistake by inventing an adjustment somewhere else.
help.approvals.title: Submitting and approving a week
help.backup.body:
A backup is a single JSON file holding your customers, projects, assignments, time entries and expenses.

You can take the whole thing, or only part of it — one customer, one project, or one date range. A partial backup is a normal backup file; it simply contains less.

Restoring **merges**: a record that is already present is skipped rather than duplicated, so restoring the same file twice is harmless and restoring an old backup does not delete newer work.

Automatic backups are off unless enabled in the configuration file. Writing copies of your data on a schedule you did not ask for is your decision to make.
help.backup.title: Backup and restore
help.editing.body:
The pencil on any row opens the entry for correction. The commonest mistake is a duration in the wrong unit - **8m** where **8h** was meant - so the duration is shown in the same notation it accepts, and the day and start time are shown beside it.

An end time, if you give one, is used instead of the duration. It is left empty on the form for that reason: a prefilled end time would silently overrule a duration you had just corrected.

Every change is recorded in the audit trail, including what the value was before, so a figure that has been corrected can still be explained later.

If the week has been submitted or approved, the entry cannot be changed until the week is withdrawn or reopened.
help.editing.title: Correcting an entry
help.entries.body:
Every entry in a date range, filtered as you like. This is also what every export is generated from, so a download is exactly what is on screen.

The filter lives in the URL, so a filtered view can be bookmarked or sent to a colleague.

**CSV** is UTF-8 with a byte order mark, so Excel on Windows reads non-ASCII customer names correctly. **JSON** follows a documented, versioned schema and carries both the recorded and the billable duration along with the rounding rule that produced it, so a downstream system can verify the arithmetic rather than trust it.
help.entries.title: Entries and export
help.expenses.body:
**Billable** and **reimbursable** are separate questions, and this application never conflates them.

A taxi you paid for and re-charge to the client is both. A hotel the client booked directly is neither. Your own train ticket on an internal project is reimbursable but not billable.

Because they are separate, reports total them separately: billable expenses join the invoice, reimbursable ones are money owed back to a person.

A markup percentage applies only to the billable side, and the billed amount is frozen when the expense is recorded — the same reasoning that freezes a rate onto a time entry.
help.expenses.title: Expenses
help.idle.body:
While a timer is running, this page watches for two things it can honestly see: that it stopped running — your machine slept, or the browser suspended the tab — and that it ran with nothing typed or clicked in it.

Neither of those means you were away, and neither is treated as though it did. A page cannot see which application you are using, so what gets recorded is what was observed, not a conclusion about it.

While the timer is still going you get a notice. Once it stops, the day view asks, and there are three answers:

- **Keep it** — it was work. Nothing changes.
- **Split** — the entry ends where the stretch began, and a second entry covers what came after it. This is the one you want when you came back and carried on.
- **Discard** — the entry ends where the stretch began, and *everything after it* is dropped as well. Each button says how much time it would leave behind, so check the number before pressing this one.

Nothing is ever removed until you press one of those. An administrator can turn the whole thing off, or change how long a stretch has to be, in Settings.
help.idle.title: Time the application saw nothing during
help.inbox.body:
A colleague can record time in your name — useful when you worked together and one of you tracks time properly.

It does not become your time until you say so. Until you accept, the entry counts for nothing: not in your totals, not in a report, not on an invoice.

You can accept it, edit it and then accept, or reject it with a reason. A rejected proposal is kept rather than deleted, so the record of what was claimed survives the disagreement.
help.inbox.title: Time proposed for you
help.month.body:
A calendar of the month with the hours on each day, which is the shape to look at when the question is about the shape of the month rather than about one day: which days have nothing on them, whether last month was busier, whether the Friday before a holiday was actually worked.
Every square links to its day and every row links to its week, so it is also the fastest way to reach a date that is not near today.
Days with nothing recorded are left blank rather than shown as zero: the gaps are the point of the view. A day marked with ! holds an entry flagged for review, which counts towards nothing until somebody looks at it.
Below the calendar is what the month went on, longest first - the answer the calendar cannot give.
help.month.title: The month overview
help.quickadd.body:
One line becomes one entry:

`2h acme/migration fixed the login redirect #travel`

Read in order: a leading duration or time range, then an assignment, then any `#tags`, and whatever remains is the note.

Durations accept `1.5`, `1,5`, `1h30`, `90m` and `1:30`. A bare whole number means minutes, because `30` almost always means half an hour. A time range like `9:00-10:30` sets the start and end instead.

Assignment names are matched against what you have worked on recently, so a fragment is usually enough. If more than one matches, or nothing does, the full form opens pre-filled rather than the tool guessing — a wrong guess that silently becomes billable time is worse than a second click.
help.quickadd.title: Quick add
help.reminders.body:
From late afternoon, the day and week views point out four things worth a look before you finish:

- a timer still running
- a day with nothing recorded on it
- time a colleague has recorded on your behalf, which counts for nothing until you decide about it
- a week that has not been submitted

None of these is sent anywhere. There is no mail, no notification and nothing scheduled: each one is worked out from your timesheet at the moment the page is drawn, which is why one can never appear about a timer you stopped a minute ago. Record the time and the reminder is simply no longer true.

The week reminder waits for the last working day of the week, because every week is unsubmitted on a Wednesday. A week with nothing recorded in it is never mentioned at all — that was a holiday, not an oversight.

**Dismiss** hides one until tomorrow, or until next week for the weekly one. An administrator can change the hour they start from, or turn them off, in Settings.
help.reminders.title: Reminders
help.seeguide: How to do things → the guide
help.themes.body:
Seven themes: light, dark, gold, sand, spring, autumn and high contrast. The choice is stored against your account, so it follows you to another device.

The high-contrast theme meets WCAG 2.1 AA contrast ratios and is verified by an automated test, so a future change to the colours cannot quietly break it.

Every screen works without a mouse. Press the shortcut key shown in the footer for the full list. Colour is never the only carrier of meaning — status always has a label or an icon as well as a hue.
help.themes.title: Themes and accessibility
help.title: Help
help.today.body:
Everything recorded for one day, with running timers at the top and both totals above the list.

Several timers may run at once, because work genuinely happens in parallel — a build running for one client while a meeting for another is under way. Overlapping entries are recorded exactly as they happened and never split between assignments automatically, because a split would be a guess that ends up on an invoice.

That is why two totals are shown. **Tracked** is the sum of every entry, and it is what gets billed. **Elapsed** is how much of the day was covered by at least one entry. When they differ, the difference is shown as **Overlap** — it is information, not an error.

Gaps between entries are marked as unaccounted time. They are prompts, never filled in for you.
help.today.title: The day view
help.users.body:
Four roles. An **admin** can do everything. A **manager** owns the customers and projects they are a member of, approves timesheets and sees money. A **member** records their own time and reads the projects they belong to. A **client** gets read-only reports for their own customer and nothing else.

The role is only half of it: **project membership** is what scopes what each person actually sees. A manager with no memberships sees nothing, which is deliberate — a new account starts with the least privilege and someone has to grant access explicitly.

Changing a role, disabling an account or changing a password signs that person out everywhere immediately. A privilege change that leaves old sessions running has not taken effect.
help.users.title: Users and access
help.week.body:
A grid of assignments against days, which is the shape most timesheets are approved in.

Rows are ordered by customer and then by name, and stay in that order between weeks, so the grid can be read across time rather than reshuffling on every visit.

Cell values are decimal hours, the form invoicing systems expect. The day totals along the bottom are summed time, matching the **Tracked** figure rather than elapsed coverage.

routines.delete.confirm: Delete this routine? Time already recorded from it is untouched.
routines.empty: No routines yet. Add one for anything you record most weeks.
routines.intro: Time that recurs: lunch, the stand-up, Friday admin. A routine is a template — nothing is recorded until you click it on the day, so the tool never invoices an hour nobody worked.
routines.name: Routine
routines.start.help: Optional. Left empty, the entry is placed at the start of the working day.

rules.expense.markup.help: Added to the billable side only. The reimbursed amount is always the cost.
rules.intro: Terms beyond the base hourly rate. Every field is optional: left empty, this customer bills exactly as it would without any of them.
rules.mileage.help: Set this and a distance can be claimed directly, priced without anyone doing the multiplication by hand.
rules.overtime.help: What an hour is worth once it is beyond the agreed working time.
rules.overtime.multiplier: Overtime as % of the base rate
rules.overtime.multiplier.help: 150 is time and a half, 200 is double time. Left empty, overtime bills at the ordinary rate.
rules.overtime.rate.help: An absolute rate. If set, it is used instead of the multiplier below.
rules.overtime.threshold.help: These only produce a reminder. Nothing is reclassified automatically: whether an hour counts as overtime is a contractual decision, not one this tool should make on your behalf.
rules.receipt.help: A week cannot be submitted while an expense above this amount has no receipt attached.
rules.reimbursement.help: What gets paid back, at what markup, and against what evidence.

rules.travel.help: Time spent travelling for this customer, recorded in full either way.
rules.travel.multiplier: Travel as % of the base rate
rules.travel.multiplier.help: 50 bills travel at half the ordinary rate. Used when no absolute travel rate is set.

settings.backuppassword.clear: Remove the password and stop encrypting backups
settings.backuppassword.help: Set a password and every backup archive is encrypted with AES-256, readable by any archiver that supports encrypted zip files. Leave it empty for a plain archive. The password is stored so scheduled backups can use it, and it protects the archive once it has left this machine - not the database it was made from.
settings.backuppassword.set: A password is set - type to replace it
settings.backuppassword.unset: No password - archives are not encrypted
settings.daypane.help: Which hours the timeline shows before anything is recorded.
settings.formats.help: Both languages write dates as 2026-08-19 unless told otherwise. It is the one order that cannot be misread: 03/04 means different days on either side of the Atlantic.
settings.idle: Watch for time the application sees nothing during
settings.idle.hint: A running timer whose page stops running, or sits untouched, for longer than this is reported for review. Nothing is ever removed without you saying so.
settings.intro: These apply to everyone using this instance.

settings.overflow.arrows: Keep the hours fixed and mark it
settings.overflow.arrows.help: An hour is always the same height. Time outside the window is reported above and below the pane instead of drawn.
settings.overflow.expand: Grow the pane to cover it
settings.overflow.expand.help: Everything recorded is drawn. An occasional late evening stretches the scale for that day.
settings.reminderhour: Start reminding from (hour of the day)
settings.reminders.hint: Nudges about a timer left running, a day with nothing on it, time a colleague recorded for you, and a week nobody has submitted. They are worked out when a screen is drawn, never sent anywhere, and each can be waved away for the day.

users.access.intro: Membership is what scopes a manager's or member's view. Someone with no memberships sees only their own records. The optional rate is that person's rate on that project, sitting between the assignment and the project in the resolution order.
users.intro: A new account starts as a member with no project memberships, so it can see nothing but its own timesheet until access is granted below. Changing a role or disabling an account signs that person out everywhere immediately.
